title: User-defined routes
learningObjective: Create route tables and user-defined routes, associate them with subnets, and predict which route Azure selects.
foundation: Azure automatically routes traffic between subnets, peered VNets, on-premises and the internet using system routes.
A user-defined route (UDR) overrides that, for example to send all traffic through a firewall.
engineer: Route table: a resource with routes (address prefix → next hop type), associated with one or more subnets (in the same region and subscription). A subnet has at most one route table.
Next hop types: Virtual appliance (an IP address of an NVA or Azure Firewall), Virtual network gateway, Virtual network, Internet, None (drop).
Selection: longest prefix match first; if prefixes are equal, user-defined routes win over BGP routes, which win over system routes.
An NVA must have IP forwarding enabled on its NIC (and forwarding in its OS) to pass traffic for other destinations.
Propagate gateway routes: disable it on a route table to stop BGP routes from on-premises being added to a subnet (for example to force everything through the firewall).
Service tags can be used as the address prefix of a route (for example Storage).

example.title: Forced tunnelling through Azure Firewall
body: Route table rt-spokes with 0.0.0.0/0 → Virtual appliance 10.0.1.4 (Azure Firewall private IP) is associated with every spoke subnet. Internet traffic is inspected and logged before leaving.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription and a resource group (rg-net)
permissions: Network Contributor on the resource group
portal: Create a resource > Route table; set Propagate gateway routes.
Route table > Routes > Add: prefix 0.0.0.0/0, next hop Virtual appliance, address 10.1.0.4.
NVA NIC > IP configurations > IP forwarding: Enabled.
configuration.cli:
az network route-table create -g rg-net -n rt-app
az network route-table route create -g rg-net --route-table-name rt-app -n default-to-fw --address-prefix 0.0.0.0/0 --next-hop-type VirtualAppliance --next-hop-ip-address 10.1.0.4
az network vnet subnet update -g rg-net --vnet-name vnet-app -n snet-app --route-table rt-app
az network nic update -g rg-net -n nva-nic --ip-forwarding true
az network nic show-effective-route-table -g rg-net -n vm-app-nic -o table
configuration.powershell:
$rt = New-AzRouteTable -Name rt-app -ResourceGroupName rg-net -Location eastus
Add-AzRouteConfig -RouteTable $rt -Name default-to-fw -AddressPrefix 0.0.0.0/0 -NextHopType VirtualAppliance -NextHopIpAddress 10.1.0.4 | Set-AzRouteTable
$vnet = Get-AzVirtualNetwork -Name vnet-app -ResourceGroupName rg-net
Set-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig -VirtualNetwork $vnet -Name snet-app -AddressPrefix 10.1.1.0/24 -RouteTable $rt | Set-AzVirtualNetwork
Get-AzEffectiveRouteTable -NetworkInterfaceName vm-app-nic -ResourceGroupName rg-net

lab.objective: Route traffic through an NVA and predict route selection.
steps: Run the default internet test and read why the NVA drops it.
Apply 'Inspect traffic to the DB subnet' (a more specific route wins).
Apply 'Route table not associated' and 'Black-hole a prefix'.
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: Traffic doesn't go through the firewall.
troubleshooting.cause: Route table not associated, or a more specific system/BGP route wins.
troubleshooting.fix: Check Effective routes on the NIC.

troubleshooting.symptom: Traffic reaches the NVA but goes no further.
troubleshooting.cause: IP forwarding disabled on the NIC or in the OS.
Return traffic bypasses the stateful firewall.
troubleshooting.fix: Add matching UDRs on the return path.

comparisons.difference: Also associated with subnets; next hops are gateways, NAT, ENIs or Transit Gateway.
Exchanges BGP routes with NVAs dynamically instead of static UDRs.

misconceptions.myth: A UDR always beats a system route.
misconceptions.reality: Only for equal prefixes; a longer prefix always wins.

architectureDecisions: Use Azure Firewall with 0.0.0.0/0 UDRs for centralised egress.
Keep route tables few and shared where possible.
Verify with Effective routes and Next hop after each change.

walkthrough.subtitle: Change where traffic goes, for example through a firewall, with your own routes.
learn: Route tables and next hop types
Routing through a network virtual appliance

steps.label: Uninspected
steps.title: Traffic goes straight out to the internet
body: Security wants every packet from the app subnet to pass through a firewall first.

steps.label: System routes
steps.title: Azure already routes for you
body: System routes send traffic within the VNet, to peered VNets, to VPN gateways and to the internet, automatically. You see them in a NIC's Effective routes.

steps.label: Route table
steps.title: A route table overrides them
body: Create a route table, add routes (address prefix + next hop), and associate it with subnets. Next hop types: Virtual appliance (an IP address), Virtual network gateway, Virtual network, Internet, or None (drop).

steps.label: Which route
steps.title: Which route wins?
body: The most specific prefix wins (a /24 beats a /16). If prefixes are equal: user-defined route, then BGP route, then system route.

callout.text: Use Network Watcher Next hop to see which route a packet will use.

steps.label: NVA
steps.title: Making an appliance work
body: Enable IP forwarding on the appliance's NIC in Azure, and inside its operating system. Remember the return path: routes are needed in both directions, or traffic becomes asymmetric and is dropped.

callout.text: Route tables apply to whole subnets, not to single VMs.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: User-defined routes
body: Your routes beat Azure's, most specific first.
recap: Route table → routes → associate to subnets
Next hops: appliance, gateway, VNet, Internet, None
Longest prefix wins; then UDR > BGP > system
Enable IP forwarding on the NVA NIC

handsOn.title: Send a subnet's internet traffic nowhere, then prove it with Next hop
handsOn.cost: Low. One B1s VM costs about US$0.01 per hour. Delete the same day.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

A virtual network vnet-lab (10.10.0.0/16) in rg-az104-lab with a subnet snet-app (10.10.1.0/24): Virtual networks > + Create > IP addresses tab. For these labs, untick 'Enable private subnet' on snet-app so lab VMs can reach the internet (in production use a NAT gateway instead).

A small Linux VM vm-lab in snet-app of vnet-lab: Virtual machines > + Create. Image Ubuntu 24.04, size Standard_B1s, password authentication, Networking tab: vnet-lab / snet-app, public IP: None, NIC network security group: Basic, public inbound ports: None. If the VM cannot reach the internet later, its subnet is private (the default for new networks): open the virtual network > Subnets, untick 'Enable private subnet', save, then stop and start the VM. In production use a NAT gateway instead.

steps.do: Open vm-lab > Networking > the NIC > Help > Effective routes.
steps.see: System routes: the VNet range with next hop Virtual network, and 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop Internet.

steps.do: Search 'Route tables' > + Create. Group rg-az104-lab, name rt-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you). Create.
Open rt-lab > Settings > Routes > + Add. Name: block-internet, destination 0.0.0.0/0 (IP addresses), next hop type: None. Add.
Open rt-lab > Subnets > + Associate: vnet-lab / snet-app. OK.
Check the NIC's Effective routes again.
steps.see: 0.0.0.0/0 now shows source User and next hop None; the system route shows as Invalid.

steps.do: Search 'Network Watcher' > Network diagnostic tools > Next hop. VM: vm-lab, destination IP 8.8.8.8. Next hop.
steps.see: Next hop type: None, and the route table rt-lab named as the reason.

steps.do: Change the route's next hop to Virtual appliance with IP 10.10.1.100 and run Next hop again.

check: Effective routes and Next hop both show your user-defined route winning.
cleanup: Dissociate rt-lab from the subnet, or: When you finish for the day: Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete. This removes everything inside it.
